meta.title: Window Film and Your HOA in Nevada | BC Glass & Tint
meta.description: Nevada law protects your right to add shutters for energy costs. It does not say the same about window film. Here is what NRS 116.2111 actually says and how to get film approved.

hero.heading: Window Film and Your HOA in Nevada
hero.intro: If your home sits in a community association anywhere in the Las Vegas valley, from Green Valley and Anthem to Seven Hills, Inspirada, Cadence and Lake Las Vegas, the question is almost always the same: am I even allowed to put film on my windows? Nevada's common-interest ownership law answers part of that, and your association's own documents answer the rest. Below is what the statute actually says, section by section, with each one cited so you can read it yourself. This is not legal advice.

statute.heading: What the Statute Says
statute.sub: Five provisions of NRS 116.2111, the section of Nevada's Common-Interest Ownership Act that governs alterations to a home inside an association. Each is taken from the statute text itself.

items.term: Changing the outside appearance of your home requires the association's permission.
items.detail: The statute says an owner may not change the appearance of the common elements, or the exterior appearance of a unit or any other portion of the common-interest community, without permission of the association. Film that is visible from outside falls under that sentence.
items.source: Source: Nevada Revised Statutes 116.2111, subsection 1, paragraph (b).

items.term: Nevada law names four things an association may not unreasonably restrict, and they are a short list.
items.detail: The statute bars an association from unreasonably restricting, prohibiting or withholding approval for an owner to add: improvements such as ramps, railings or elevators needed for a resident with a disability; additional locks to improve security; shutters to improve security or to reduce the cost of energy; and a wind energy system where the property is two acres or more.
items.source: Source: Nevada Revised Statutes 116.2111, subsection 2, paragraph (c).

items.term: Window film is not on that list.
items.detail: We read the full text of NRS Chapter 116 and searched it end to end. The words film and tint do not appear anywhere in the chapter. That is not a loophole and it is not a prohibition either. It means film is handled by your association's own governing documents rather than by a protection written into state law.
items.source: Source: Nevada Revised Statutes Chapter 116, full chapter text, read 28 August 2026.

items.term: Shutters get a second, stronger protection that film does not get.
items.detail: The statute devotes an entire additional subsection to shutters, including rolling shutters, and to the owner's right to attach them for security or to reduce energy costs. Nothing equivalent exists for window film. If a neighbor tells you the law protects any energy-saving window product, this is the provision they are thinking of, and it is about shutters.

items.term: Anything visible has to follow your association's own procedure and suit the look of the community.
items.detail: Improvements that are visible from elsewhere in the community must be installed in accordance with the procedures set out in the association's governing documents, and must be selected or designed to the maximum extent practicable to be compatible with the style of the community. In plain terms: fill out the architectural request, and pick a film that does not stand out.

statute.footer_note: Read the statute yourself: Nevada Revised Statutes Chapter 116, section 116.2111.

blocks.heading: What This Means When You Want Film
paragraphs: In practice, an association is rarely objecting to window film as such. It is objecting to a mirrored or reflective look that makes one house stand out from the row. That is what the compatible with the style of the community language is aimed at. So the request that gets approved is usually the boring one: a non-reflective film, submitted through the architectural review process before the work is booked, with the product named.

When you ask us for a quote on a home inside an association, tell us that up front. We will give you the film name and the finish in writing so you have something concrete to attach to the request, rather than the word tint on a blank form. We would rather wait for your approval than install something you have to take off.

blocks.heading: What We Do Not Know and Will Not Guess
paragraphs: We cannot tell you what your association will approve. Every community writes its own covenants, conditions and restrictions, and the statute leaves the detail to those documents. Two houses a mile apart in Henderson can sit under completely different rules.

We also will not quote you a reflectivity limit for your community. Those numbers live in each association's own design guidelines, they differ, and we have not verified any specific one. Ask your association for its architectural guidelines in writing, and read what it says about window treatments and exterior appearance. If it says nothing, that is worth knowing before you start, not after.
We install window film. We are not attorneys and nothing here is legal advice.

items.question: Do I need HOA approval before tinting my home windows?
items.answer: Assume yes if the film will be visible from outside. Nevada law says an owner may not change the exterior appearance of a unit without permission of the association, so the safe order is: get the film and finish in writing from us, submit your architectural request, then book the install. Source: Nevada Revised Statutes 116.2111, subsection 1, paragraph (b).

items.question: Does Nevada law protect my right to install window film to save energy?
items.answer: Not in the way it protects shutters. NRS 116.2111 bars an association from unreasonably restricting four specific additions: disability access improvements, additional locks, shutters for security or energy costs, and a wind energy system on two acres or more. Window film is not among them, and the words film and tint do not appear anywhere in NRS Chapter 116. Source: Nevada Revised Statutes 116.2111, subsection 2, paragraph (c), and the full chapter text.

items.question: Why do associations care about window film at all?
items.answer: Because of how it looks from the street. The statute asks that visible improvements be compatible with the style of the community, which is an appearance test, not a performance test. A film with a mirrored finish is the one that draws an objection. A non-reflective film usually does not. Source: Nevada Revised Statutes 116.2111, subsection 3.

items.question: What should I put on the architectural request form?
items.answer: The specific film we are installing and its finish, the windows it goes on, and who is installing it. Call or text us at 702-550-8840 and we will put that in writing for you before you submit. A form that just says tint is the one that comes back with questions.

items.question: Do you work inside HOA communities in Henderson and Las Vegas?
items.answer: Yes. Windows do not move, so residential and commercial film is mobile: we come to your home. Our shop is in Boulder City and we work throughout Henderson, Las Vegas and Southern Nevada. Vehicles come to the shop, homes we come to you.
